endorsements.quote: After establishing a baseline performance on an open-source dataset, a restricted-access benchmark dataset that has not been used for model development can then be utilized to get an estimate of the true performance of the developed AI algorithm in new, unseen cases.

It is also recommended to report confidence intervals since they are of high importance for performance metrics in biomedical research due to the extra information they provide for the samples used [ 68 ].
Reporting performance metrics for subgroups, such as by age, sex, or race [ 5 , 69 , 70 ], can help to assess bias and identify specific subgroups in which the model might underperform.

Furthermore, information about specific subgroups and the data used to develop an algorithm can be provided through Model Cards [ 76 ], helping to enhance transparency and accountability in model deployment.

Comparing AI software’s performance on benchmark datasets with that of radiologists or other expert clinicians reveals areas where AI or clinicians are superior, indicating the potential added value of the software.
Moreover, compliance with local Institutional Review Board regulations must be achieved prior to using patient data for model development/validation.
Moreover, the manuscript describing the dataset and possible use cases should follow specific reporting guidelines appropriate to the type of application [ 59 ].

unlisted_practices: Create benchmark datasets that are expert-labeled, transparently and rigorously documented, and representative of the intended clinical context, population, and disease spectrum.
Limit the number of times an algorithm can be evaluated on the same benchmark dataset, or provide different dataset fractions per run, to reduce overfitting risk.
Do not use publicly available imaging datasets to validate vendor AI software, since vendors may have trained on them and performance will be overestimated.
Preserve natural disease prevalence in benchmark datasets used to validate real-world performance.
Ensure benchmark image acquisition settings and parameters resemble intended clinical use, and assess datasets for data drift from older scanners, population, or guideline changes.
Report the experience of expert annotators and identify and analyze cases with poor interobserver agreement.
Perform sample size calculations for benchmark datasets, or consult a biostatistician.
Vet the privileges and access granted to software providers during validation, for example by local offline installation or encryption, to protect patient privacy.
Verify that de-identification of images is complete, including burnt-in patient data in DICOM images, with manual confirmation of automated removal methods.
Apply the same preprocessing steps at inference as used during algorithm training, and describe preprocessing and share code to ensure reproducibility.

screen.reason: The paper provides recommendations and guidelines for the creation and accessibility of benchmark datasets for validating AI in radiology.
